Since the beginning of November, the cost of transporting crude oil via Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) has fallen sharply. This decline reflects both weakening demand for VLCC charters and the fading of the geopolitical risk premium that had previously driven freight rates to historic highs in October.
Data from the Baltic Exchange shows that on November 13, VLCC freight rates on the Gulf of Oman to China route (as measured by the Worldscale index) fell to approximately 308 points, a sharp drop of 64% from the all-time high (841 points) reached on October 8.
As VLCC freight rates plummet, oil-exporting nations in the Gulf have ramped up their crude exports to levels seen before the onset of the U.S.-Iran conflict.

Ghost Data Centers: What Connection Queues Reveal About the Rise of AI

12 November 2026

The tensions caused by artificial intelligence data centers do not stem solely from the actual electricity consumed . Projects that are still uncertain may reserve capacity from multiple grids , lengthen connection waitlists and distort planning . The debate therefore centers just as much on the maturity of the projects and the sharing of costs that on growth, which is very real, the energy demand of digital technology.
01

What Just Happened

On October 13, 2026, The Wall Street Journal described the growing difficulty U.S. electric utilities face in distinguishing between data center projects that are ready for construction and those that are still in the exploratory phase [1] . In this context, the term “ghost data center” refers to a project announced as part of a connection queue, but for which the financing, land, equipment, timeline, or even the final location have not yet been sufficiently established.
This classification does not necessarily mean that a project is fraudulent. A single developer may explore multiple regions to compare timelines, electricity prices, or regulatory constraints. The same potential load is then counted multiple times across separate portfolios. Conversely, an overloaded grid can slow down credible projects and lead grid operators to consider upgrades that may not all ultimately be necessary.
The key point
A connection request measures an intention and a maximum need considered. It does not constitute neither observed consumption nor a guarantee of construction, nor a certain forecast of future charge.
02

What’s Really New

Speculative projects in the power grid are nothing new. What has changed with AI is their scale, geographic concentration, and speed. According to the WSJ, a typical request made to certain suppliers has increased from about 50 MW to 1,000 MW or more [1] .

...

How Does a

Connection Queue Work?
When a project requires high power capacity, the manager analyzes its location, consumption profile, start date, and the work required. The manager may need to upgrade a substation, a transmission line, or flexibility resources. The project moves forward through a series of technical studies, financial guarantees, permits, and contracts. Therefore, being in the queue does not mean that capacity is immediately available.
* Concept | What it indicates | What it does not prove
* Required power | The maximum power specified by the project. | The actual load drawn as soon as the door opens.
* Case in the queue | A request that has been filed or is under review. | Confirmed construction of the data center.
* Technical Study | Potential impacts on the network and necessary reinforcements. | Final financing for all the work.

* Indicator | Published value | Conservative estimate
* Requests deemed highly credible | 23% of applications disclosed, according to Wood Mackenzie as cited by the WSJ. | An estimate of maturity, not a universal abandonment rate.
* Exelon Portfolio | 18 GW in applications, then 11 GW deemed highly likely following commitments, with approximately $1 billion in guarantees. | The guarantees filter the queue, without ensuring that every MW will be consumed.
* ERCOT, April 2026 | Approximately 410 GW of monitored large loads, nearly 87% of which are data centers [4] . | A backlog of demand far exceeding the capacity already in service.
* Great Britain | Contractual demand has risen from 41 to 125 GW, of which approximately 73 GW is from data centers [6] . | The regulator estimates that a significant portion of this may not materialize.
* Global consumption | 415 TWh for data centers in 2024, or about 1.5% of global electricity [2] . | Consumption is real and growing, even if the figures overestimate certain projects.
These figures should not be added together, as they describe different areas, dates, and scopes. Nevertheless, they point to two common observations. The growth in electricity demand from data centers is measurable. At the same time, the gross volume of applications does not constitute a reliable projection without information on duplicates, studies conducted, guarantees submitted, and the ramp-up schedule.
06

Liability Issues

...

* ✓ Report separately the requested, planned, contracted, energized, and actually drawn power;
* ✓ Report requests submitted for the same project in multiple jurisdictions, without disclosing trade secrets;
* ✓ Require the applicant to bear a reasonable share of the risk associated with reinforcement and removal;
* ✓ Plan for a phased ramp-up, with a review of unused capacity;
* ✓ Assess local impacts on rates, water, emissions, employment, and grid resilience.

What to Watch for Now

The first useful metric will be the conversion rate of the queues: how many megawatts requested actually reach the planning, contracting, energization, and consumption stages? It will also be necessary to track the gap between reserved capacity and observed peak demand, cancellations after a security deposit has been posted, the duration of connections, and the portion of costs ultimately borne by data centers.
International comparisons will be instructive.

The Data Center Interconnection Queue: Steps, Waits and Options

How a large site asks the grid for power, why the answer takes years, and what you can do instead of waiting. Every number is sourced and dated.
Updated October 29, 2026 · By Accretion Compute team · 7 min read
Quick answer
A data center interconnection queue is the line of requests waiting for a utility or grid operator to study, approve and build the connection a large site needs. Data centers join a load queue; power plants join a separate generation queue. Studies, grid upgrades and equipment lead times push many connections out by years.
On this page
1. What the queue is
2. Steps in the process
3. Why waits are long
4. Recent reforms
5. Time to power
6. Your options
7. Where Accretion fits
8. FAQ
If you are planning AI capacity, the data center interconnection queue often sets the date that matters most. Land, buildings and chips can be bought. Power at the size you need, delivered to your fence line, has to be granted by whoever runs the local grid, and they work through requests in order.
This guide covers what the queue is, the steps a large load goes through, why the wait is long, what changed in 2025 and 2026, and the realistic ways to reach power sooner. Numbers come from FERC, DOE, Berkeley Lab and ERCOT, with the date we checked them.

What is an interconnection queue?

An interconnection queue is the list of projects that have formally asked to connect to the grid and are waiting for studies, an agreement and construction. Each request is checked for what it would do to the system and what must be built first.
What is grid interconnection? It is the physical and contractual link between a site and the electric system: lines, substation, protection equipment, and an agreement that sets how much power can flow and who pays for what.
There are two kinds of queue, and they are easy to confuse:

...

What steps does a data center grid connection go through?

Most large-load requests follow the same broad path, though each utility names the steps differently. Berkeley Lab summarizes it as inquiry, request, studies, agreement, construction and in service.
1. Inquiry. You ask the utility whether a site could take your load, and roughly when. Answers here are informal.
2. Formal request. You submit size, location, ramp schedule and in-service date. Expect to show site control and pay a study deposit.
3. Studies. The utility, and in organized markets the grid operator, models what your load does to the system. The output is a list of upgrades and a cost estimate.
4. Agreement. You sign an interconnection or service agreement setting capacity, dates, upgrades and who pays. This usually needs a larger financial commitment.
5. Construction. The utility builds or upgrades substations, lines and protection. This is where equipment lead times bite.
6. Energization and ramp. Power is switched on, often in stages, with full load allowed only as later upgrades finish.
Milestones run alongside: site control, deposits, financial commitments and long-lead equipment orders. Miss one and a request can lose its place.
How big is large? DOE's 2025 proposal to FERC defined large loads as greater than 20 MW. ERCOT treats a single site above 75 MW of peak demand as a large user. An AI campus is usually well above both. For how loads add up, see how much power a data center uses .

Why is the data center interconnection queue so long?

The queue is long because requests far outnumber what the grid can absorb quickly, and each needs studies, upgrades and equipment that take years. Five causes explain most of it.
1. Volume. Requests have outrun the system. As of June 2026, ERCOT was tracking about 474,000 MW of large-load requests, about 90% of them from data centers. Its all-time peak demand record is 91,134 MW, set in July 2026. In PJM, large-load adjustments in the 2026 forecast reach 39 GW by 2030 and 87 GW by 2040, against a peak system of 154 GW. Our data center power demand forecast guide sets the main forecasts side by side.
2. Speculative and duplicate requests. Developers often file for one project at several sites. Each request still has to be studied, and each changes the results for others. The generation side shows how few requests become projects: of capacity that applied from 2000 to 2020, only 13% was operating by the end of 2025 and 75% had withdrawn.
3. Studies and restudies. Studied one at a time, each new project can change the answer for those already in line. ERCOT says this triggered costly restudies that delayed timelines, which is why it moved to batch studies.

...

Does a place in the queue guarantee power?

No. A queue position only means your request is being studied. Rights to capacity come with a signed agreement, met milestones and finished upgrades. Requests can still be withdrawn or restudied. On the generation side, Berkeley Lab found withdrawal rates above 40% even after signing an agreement.

Daniel Opoku

Daniel Opoku

19 Nov 2026 — 11 min read
Share

...

European drone manufacturers face growing pressure to prove where their components originate. But eliminating dependence on Chinese supply chains requires more than transparent sourcing and stricter procurement rules. It requires industrial investment, reliable alternatives, and governments willing to help build them.
A European defense ministry can order a domestically manufactured drone. What it cannot do, simply by writing new conditions into a procurement contract, is create a European factory capable of producing every critical component inside it.
That distinction is becoming increasingly important as Europe accelerates military drone production and introduces new requirements intended to strengthen its defense industrial base.
